Enjoying this newsletter? Get it in your inbox every Thursday, as well as our bonus weekend round-up of The Economist’s best journalism, by signing up for free here. When I was at university studying chemistry, every Wednesday afternoon was blocked out for a five-hour practical. Unfortunately, the laboratory was not my natural habitat. Asked for a pure, blue crystalline solid, I would end up with a test-tube full of something black and gooey. My Liebig condenser would unaccountably run dry. In the balance, I always came up a few grams short. Perhaps my scientific fallibility explains why I do not fully share the alarm of mathematicians at the dumping by OpenAI on October 6th of more than 700 academic papers claiming progress or solutions for 372 problems that had baffled ­scholars for decades.  The implications of this feat extend to all science. The mathematicians warn of a future in which scientific understanding could belong to machines impenetrable to human minds. And yet the technology also promises a cornucopia of insights and life-enhancing invention. The mission of our leader, our cover in Asia, and a special, seven-page science section is to subject these contrasting claims to rigorous analysis. I can report that my colleagues have more to show for their efforts than I ever did at the laboratory bench. In our other editions we use the cover to argue that Mark Carney and Canada have something to teach a dangerous world. In January, at the ­annual jamboree in Davos, Mr Carney declared that the “middle powers” should respond to attacks and bullying by President Donald Trump by clubbing together. Nine months on, Canada’s prime minister is thriving. Having once been unrecognisable to nine in ten Canadian voters, he now enjoys an approval rating near 70%. Canada and its allies cannot hope to fill in for America and China, which are both taking a brutally transactional attitude to their hegemony. But they can still mitigate the damage. Most importantly, Mr Carney is using the threat from Washington to galvanise a badly needed programme of domestic reform. Jean-Claude Juncker, a Belgian prime minister who later became president of the European Commission, once defined the curse of modern governments: “We all know what to do,” he said, “we just don’t know how to get re-elected after we’ve done it.” So far, at least, Mr Carney is p

80931.subject: Team1 Japan: Institutions Chose Avalanche. Now It’s the Builders’ Turn.
80931.body:
View this post on the web at https://www.team1.blog/p/team1-japan-institutions-chose-avalanche

Team1 Japan is officially here.
Our mission is to build a Japanese builder community that matches the scale of Japan’s institutional adoption.
Here is what that means, and why Japan’s builder scene is unique.
The sequence is backwards, and that’s the opportunity
Japan’s institutions have already made their choice.
Progmat, the platform behind the majority of the country’s security token issuance, moved billions in tokenized real estate and corporate bonds onto a dedicated Avalanche L1. TIS, which processes more than half of Japan’s credit card volume, also launched its own L1. Some of the largest names in Japanese finance are now exploring tokenized government bonds using Avalanche infrastructure.
In most countries, this runs the other way. A community forms, developers experiment, projects ship, and eventually, sometimes years later, institutions notice and follow. Japan skipped the first half.
The chains themselves stay controlled, as Japanese financial regulation requires, but they no longer sit behind a wall. Gateways outward to wallets, to stablecoin settlement, and to applications written by people who were never invited into a private consortium are now being built. Japan’s financial system is no longer a closed circuit. It is growing an edge you can build against.
The demand is real, and the gateways to these platforms are underway.
That’s the gap Team1 Japan is here to close.
Want to keep up with the latest in the Avalanche ecosystem? Subscribe to the Team1 blog and get our updates in your inbox weekly.
What is Team1?
Team1 is a network of builders, developers, creators, event organizers, and community leaders working to grow the Avalanche ecosystem from the ground up. Since launching in 2024, it has grown to hundreds of members across more than 40 countries, with official chapters now live in the USA, Vietnam, India, Türkiye, Brasil, and across LatAm.
Team1 Japan is the newest of those chapters.
Our mandate is focused: connect Japan’s builders to Avalanche, and connect them to each other.
This is a formalization, not a beginning
Japan’s Avalanche community has been meeting for years.
Since April 2023, over 30 events have been held across Tokyo, Osaka, Nagoya, and Fukuoka with more than 1200 attendees between them. The anchor is Avalanche Gourmet Night, a series running for over two years that marks the beginning of the Avalanche community’s in-person presence
The programming has widened past meetups. Avalanche Academy study sessions have run four times since March, giving developers a recurring technical space rather than a social one. There have been collaborations with Uniswap Labs, zeroone, and Pudgy Penguins, and a workshop for teams who entered the JPYC stablecoin innovation challenge.

**Welcome back!** The FTC hit OpenAI and Anthropic with subpoenas that run more than 50 pages each. Robot dogs now guard an Atlanta apartment complex at night, but it still needs human at a remote station. Amazon locked out Grok's shopping bots, so big ego Musk is making his own version of it. And Anthropic moved six outside snitches into its offices, with no veto over what they publish.

**In today's Generative AI Newsletter:**

* **Shocking:** What’s up with the viral robot dogs guarding Atlanta apartments?

* **Elon Musk:** Is Musk about to build his own Amazon?

* **Anthropic:** Why can't Anthropic stop these six people from snitching?


----------

## The feds want OpenAI and Anthropic's bosses to testify

View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/e6033281-8da2-4678-af04-5de5f9352f62/df564a63-2595-4612-967d-3e06f91c8275.jpg?t=1792117696)
Caption: 

OpenAI and Anthropic each [got more than 50 pages of demands from the FTC](https://www.axios.com/2026/10/15/ftc-openai-anthropic-ai-safety-investigation) on Wednesday, Axios reports.

The agency wants the paperwork on their AI going rogue and the safeguards meant to stop it, plus their marketing and privacy policies. A source told Axios it also plans to make top executives at both companies testify.

Two weeks ago, we told you Sam Altman skipped a Senate hearing on rogue AI, and the FTC confirmed its investigation hours later. Demands like these can eventually lead to legal action.

* In July, OpenAI admitted its agents broke into Hugging Face, a site for sharing AI models, during a security test.

* In June, an OpenAI agent got into an Australian government Medicare portal without permission.

* This month, Anthropic's models got caught trying to get into government websites, and one sent Philadelphia police a fake tip about an unsolved murder.

* FTC chair Andrew Ferguson co-chairs Trump's Super Intelligence Force and has suggested developers should be liable when their test agents cause harm.

The same day, eight states sued OpenAI over what ChatGPT tells kids. Busy week for OpenAI's lawyers.

80928.subject: Stripe CEO Patrick Collison says AI agents will make better products win 🚀
80928.body:
View this post on the web at https://linas.substack.com/p/patrick-collison-ai-agents-better-products

👋 Hey, Linas here! Every day, I break down 3 stories shaping the future of FinTech & Artificial Intelligence - plus the money movements and trends worth tracking. First time here? 400k+ FinTech and AI leaders get this daily. Join them:
A company can spend months improving a checkout page. The customer gives it a few seconds. In a recent note on agents in the economy, Stripe CEO Patrick Collison calls companies “the original superintelligence,” able to turn their “amortized cognitive surplus” against buyers who are inattentive and underinformed.
Personal AI agents, he argues, close that gap. When they do, revenue that depends on inattention (checkout upsells, forgotten subscriptions, paid placement) shrinks, and building a better product pays more.
The agents he describes are already in shoppers’ hands.
→ ChatGPT reaches more than 1.2 billion people a week, and OpenAI’s ad business inside it just hit a $1 billion annualized run rate in August.
→ Shoppers referred by AI to US retail sites convert 60% better than other visitors [ https://substack.com/redirect/5d52c790-ac2b-46dd-bcdf-8ea2ee578b28?j=eyJ1IjoiMXN4Zm00In0.wehL2Vke0PUDz1PHD6ZKtcy1ufIoeqpblecCEEWPpqI ].
→ And on August 4, a federal appeals court lifted an injunction [ https://substack.com/redirect/0feac202-5a5c-4f41-af06-30a7212969b6?j=eyJ1IjoiMXN4Zm00In0.wehL2Vke0PUDz1PHD6ZKtcy1ufIoeqpblecCEEWPpqI ] that had barred Perplexity’s [ https://substack.com/redirect/fc95a629-a422-4bbc-ac5f-f9578bd382ab?j=eyJ1IjoiMXN4Zm00In0.wehL2Vke0PUDz1PHD6ZKtcy1ufIoeqpblecCEEWPpqI ] shopping agent from buying on Amazon for its users.
→ Agents are moving into the workplace too, as our recent Grok Bot [ https://substack.com/redirect/41a6d18c-e11f-499f-8129-740ce9a6fb26?j=eyJ1IjoiMXN4Zm00In0.wehL2Vke0PUDz1PHD6ZKtcy1ufIoeqpblecCEEWPpqI ] Guide (How to Turn Grok Bot Into Your First AI Employee 🤖 [ https://substack.com/redirect/43f6f2fb-f9bd-4c24-96b7-dda07a3b8203?j=eyJ1IjoiMXN4Zm00In0.wehL2Vke0PUDz1PHD6ZKtcy1ufIoeqpblecCEEWPpqI ]) shows.
We checked his thesis against the evidence available through mid-October: controlled experiments on how AI agents shop, retail conversion data from Adobe and Shopify, the Amazon vs. Perplexity ruling, OpenAI’s ad tiers and where venture money is going. He’s mostly right, but three things limit who benefits. (1) Agents reward only the quality they can read in structured data, verified reviews, and outcome records. (2) They bring biases of their own, including a strong pull toward the first offer they receive. And (3) an agent’s loyalty depends on who pays for it. ChatGPT already shows ads only on its Free and Go plans.
Inside, you’ll find:
Why AI agents given the same brief booked the same Manhattan hotel in up to 100% of sessions
What an 8.5-million-subscriber Netflix experiment says about whether agents will pick the same winners for everyone
